questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The free electrons in a metal wire 2.0 m long have a mobility of 4.0 × 10⁻³ m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. A potential difference of 3.0 V is maintained between the ends of the wire. The drift speed of the electrons is:

solution.concept: Mobility: µ = v_d/E, so v_d = µE with E = V/L
solution.explanation: Mobility is the drift speed per unit electric field. The field in a uniform wire is the potential difference divided by the length.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.2 × 10⁻² m/s multiplies µ by V instead of by E. 2.4 × 10⁻² m/s multiplies by the length instead of dividing. 2.7 × 10⁻³ m/s divides µ by E.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', mobility

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Four identical cells, each of emf 1.5 V and internal resistance 0.4 Ω, are connected in parallel (all positive terminals joined together). A 1.4 Ω resistor is connected across the combination. The current in the resistor is:

solution.concept: Identical cells in parallel: emf ε, internal resistance r/n
solution.explanation: Connecting identical cells in parallel does not raise the emf; it only divides the internal resistance by the number of cells.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 A treats the cells as being in series (6 V, 1.6 Ω). 0.83 A uses the internal resistance of one cell (0.4 Ω) instead of 0.1 Ω. 4.0 A adds the emfs as in series but divides the internal resistance as in parallel.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells in series and in parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform wire of resistance 12 Ω is bent into a complete circle. The resistance between two diametrically opposite points of the circle is:

solution.concept: Two halves of the ring in parallel
solution.explanation: Between two diametrically opposite points, the ring is two semicircular wires, each of half the total resistance, joined in parallel.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 Ω counts only one semicircle. 12 Ω is the resistance of the straight wire. 24 Ω adds the two halves as if in series with the whole wire.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors in series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A power station delivers 400 kW to a distant town through transmission cables whose total resistance is 5 Ω. The power is transmitted at 20 kV. The power lost as heat in the cables is:

solution.concept: Power loss in connecting wires: P_loss = I²R_c with I = P/V
solution.explanation: The current in the cables is fixed by the power delivered and the transmission voltage; the heat produced in the cables depends on this current and on their resistance. The 20 kV is not the voltage across the cables.
solution.why_others_wrong: 80 MW uses V²/R_c, treating the full 20 kV as if it were across the cables. 100 W is I × R_c, which is the voltage drop in the cables (100 V), not a power. 2000 MW forgets to convert 20 kV to volts (I = 20 000 A).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electrical energy and power (power loss in transmission)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A copper wire is at room temperature and no electric field is applied to it. The average velocity of all the free electrons in the wire is:

options.text: of the order of 10⁵ m/s, directed along the length of the wire
zero, because their thermal velocities are randomly directed
of the order of 10⁻⁴ m/s, directed along the length of the wire
equal to the speed of light in copper

solution.concept: Random thermal motion of free electrons
solution.explanation: Free electrons move with large thermal speeds, but their directions are random, so their velocities average to zero. Only when a field is applied does a small drift velocity get superposed on this random motion.
steps: Thermal speeds are large but randomly directed
With no field, there is no drift and no current
solution.why_others_wrong: 10⁵ m/s is the order of the thermal speed of an individual electron, not the average velocity. 10⁻⁴ m/s is a typical drift speed, which exists only when a field is applied. The speed of light is unrelated.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option B: zero, because their thermal velocities are randomly directed

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II for a metallic conductor (n = number density of free electrons, e = electronic charge, m = electron mass, τ = relaxation time, E = electric field, A = cross-sectional area, v_d = drift speed).

List-I:
A. Magnitude of the drift velocity
B. Current in the conductor
C. Resistivity
D. Conductivity

List-II:
I. ne²τ/m
II. eEτ/m
III. m/(ne²τ)
IV. neAv_d

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Drude picture of conduction
solution.explanation: An electron accelerates as eE/m between collisions, giving an average drift eEτ/m. The charge crossing a section per second is neAv_d. Substituting gives J = (ne²τ/m)E, so σ = ne²τ/m and ρ = 1/σ = m/(ne²τ).
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping C and D confuses resistivity with its reciprocal. The other codes put a current or a drift speed against the wrong formula.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A cell of emf 6 V and internal resistance 1 Ω and a cell of emf 2 V and internal resistance 1 Ω are connected in a single loop with a 2 Ω resistor. The cells oppose each other: the positive terminal of one is joined to the positive terminal of the other. The potential difference across the terminals of the 2 V cell is:

solution.concept: A cell being charged: V = ε + Ir
solution.explanation: The net emf drives current in the direction set by the 6 V cell, so current is forced into the 2 V cell at its positive terminal; that cell is being charged and its terminal voltage exceeds its emf.
steps: 2 V cell is charged: V = ε + Ir = 2 + 1 × 1 = 3 V
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 V uses V = ε − Ir, which applies to a cell that is discharging. 2 V ignores the drop across the internal resistance. 5 V is the terminal voltage of the 6 V cell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a metre bridge, a resistance X is in the left gap and a resistance R in the right gap, and the null point is 40.0 cm from the left end of the wire. When a 5 Ω resistor is connected in series with X in the left gap (R unchanged), the null point moves to 50.0 cm from the left end. The value of X is:

solution.concept: Metre bridge balance: (left resistance)/(right resistance) = l/(100 − l)
solution.explanation: Write the balance condition for both positions of the null point and solve the two equations for X and R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15 Ω is the value of R. 20 Ω comes from taking X/(X + 5) = 40/50, i.e. using the two balance lengths as if R were not needed. 5 Ω assumes X equals the added resistor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', meter bridge

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform wire of resistance 10 Ω is cut into five pieces of equal length, and the five pieces are then connected in parallel. The resistance of the combination is:

solution.concept: Cutting a wire divides its resistance; parallel combination of equal resistors
solution.explanation: Each piece has one-fifth of the length and hence one-fifth of the resistance. Five equal resistors in parallel have one-fifth of the resistance of one of them.
steps: Five 2 Ω pieces in parallel: 2/5 = 0.4 Ω (in general R/n²)
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 Ω is the resistance of a single piece. 50 Ω multiplies by 5 instead of dividing. 0.08 Ω divides by 5 three times (R/n³).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a part of a circuit, a steady current of 2 A flows from point A to point B through the following elements in series, in this order: a 2 Ω resistor, a cell of emf 3 V and negligible internal resistance whose positive terminal faces B, and a 1 Ω resistor. The potential difference V_A − V_B is:

solution.concept: Potential changes along a branch (Kirchhoff's loop rule)
solution.explanation: Walk from A to B in the direction of the current. The potential falls by IR across each resistor and rises by ε on crossing the cell from its negative to its positive terminal.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 V treats the cell as a drop instead of a rise. 6 V ignores the cell. −3 V has the right size but the wrong sign: A is at the higher potential.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a switch is closed, a bulb several metres away lights up almost at once, although the drift speed of the free electrons in the connecting wires is only of the order of 1 mm/s.
Reason (R): An electric field is set up throughout the circuit almost instantly, so the free electrons everywhere in the wires start drifting at practically the same time.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Establishment of current in a circuit
solution.explanation: The current in the filament does not wait for electrons from the switch to arrive. The electric field spreads through the wires at nearly the speed of light, and electrons already present in every part of the circuit begin to drift together. A is true and R correctly explains it.
steps: Drift speed ~ 1 mm/s, yet the bulb lights at once → A true
The field is established along the whole circuit almost instantly → R true
Electrons in the filament start moving immediately because of the field → R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: R is exactly the reason the bulb does not have to wait for electrons to travel from the switch, so B, C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons (worked example on drift speed)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Doubling the potential difference across a metal wire kept at a constant temperature doubles its resistance.
Reason (R): At constant temperature, the current through a metal wire is directly proportional to the potential difference across it.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Ohm's law: resistance of an ohmic conductor
solution.explanation: For a metal at constant temperature, I ∝ V (Ohm's law, R is true). Doubling V therefore doubles I, and R = V/I stays the same. A is false.
steps: I ∝ V at constant temperature → R true
R = V/I unchanged when V and I both double → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options A, B and C (which need A to be true) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Electric current is a vector quantity, since it has a direction of flow.
Statement II: The relation J = σE, between the current density J and the electric field E, is an equivalent form of Ohm's law.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Current as a scalar; Ohm's law in terms of J and E
solution.explanation: Current has a sense along a wire but does not add as a vector (currents meeting at a junction add algebraically), so it is a scalar; current density J is the vector. Writing V = IR for a small element of length l and area A gives E l = J A (ρl/A), i.e. E = ρJ or J = σE, which is Ohm's law in another form.
steps: Currents add algebraically at a junction → scalar → Statement I false
V = IR → El = (JA)(ρl/A) → J = σE → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false and Statement II is true; every other combination is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', electric current; Ohm's law
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the metre bridge are correct?

(a) It works on the principle of the Wheatstone bridge.
(b) The resistors and the wire are connected by thick metal strips whose resistance can be neglected.
(c) The position of the null point does not depend on the emf of the cell used.
(d) At the null point, the current through the galvanometer is maximum.
(e) The resistance per unit length of the bridge wire must be known to calculate the unknown resistance.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Metre bridge: balance condition and construction
solution.explanation: The metre bridge is a Wheatstone bridge in which two arms are the two segments of a uniform wire. At balance no current flows through the galvanometer, and X/R = (resistance of l)/(resistance of 100 − l) = l/(100 − l), because the resistance per unit length cancels. The balance condition contains only resistances, so it does not depend on the cell's emf.
steps: (b) True: thick copper strips of negligible resistance
(c) True: balance condition has no emf in it
(d) False: galvanometer current is zero at the null point
(e) False: resistance per unit length cancels in the ratio
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes (d) or (e), which are false, or leaves out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', meter bridge

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Resistors P = 1 Ω and Q = 2 Ω are joined in series to form one branch, and R = 2 Ω and S = 1 Ω in series form a second branch. Both branches are connected across an ideal 6 V battery, with P and R joined to its positive terminal. The P–Q junction (point B) and the R–S junction (point D) are then joined by a wire of negligible resistance. The current in this wire is:

options.text: 1.5 A, flowing from D to B
1.5 A, flowing from B to D
3 A, flowing from B to D

solution.concept: Kirchhoff's junction and loop rules for an unbalanced bridge with a shorting wire
solution.explanation: The wire puts B and D at the same potential, so P and R are in parallel between the positive terminal and B/D, and Q and S are in parallel between B/D and the negative terminal. Find the common potential, then apply the junction rule at B.
steps: P ∥ R = 2/3 Ω and Q ∥ S = 2/3 Ω, so B and D are at 3 V
Current into B through P = 3/1 = 3 A; current out of B through Q = 3/2 = 1.5 A
Junction rule at B: 3 − 1.5 = 1.5 A leaves B through the wire, towards D
Check at D: 3/2 = 1.5 A in through R plus 1.5 A from the wire = 3 A out through S = 3/1 A
solution.why_others_wrong: 'From D to B' gets the direction wrong. Zero would need P/Q = R/S (a balanced bridge), but 1/2 ≠ 2/1. 3 A is the current in P, not the share that crosses the wire.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules
solution.final_answer: Option B: 1.5 A, flowing from B to D

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a metre bridge, a wire of length 50.0 cm and diameter 0.40 mm is connected in the left gap and a standard resistance of 2.0 Ω in the right gap. The null point is 60.0 cm from the left end of the bridge wire. The resistivity of the material of the wire is about:

solution.concept: Metre bridge balance, then ρ = RA/L with A = πd²/4
solution.explanation: First find the resistance of the wire from the balance length, then convert it to resistivity using the wire's own length and cross-sectional area.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.4 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m inverts the bridge ratio (X = 4/3 Ω). 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ Ω m uses the diameter as the radius. 9.6 × 10⁻⁷ Ω m takes the area as d², leaving out π/4.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', meter bridge; resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 2 Ω is connected across an external resistor R. The power dissipated in R is 16 W. The value of R is:

solution.concept: Power delivered to an external resistor: P = ε²R/(R + r)²
solution.explanation: Below the maximum power (which occurs at R = r), every value of power is delivered for two different load resistances, one smaller and one larger than r.
steps: R = 1 Ω or 4 Ω (check: 1 Ω → I = 4 A, P = 16 W; 4 Ω → I = 2 A, P = 16 W)
solution.shortcut: Maximum power here is ε²/4r = 18 W at R = 2 Ω; 16 W is below it, so expect two roots whose product is r² = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 Ω uses P = ε²/R and ignores the internal resistance. 7 Ω subtracts r from that wrong value. 2 Ω is the load for maximum power (18 W), not 16 W.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance; electrical power
solution.final_answer: Option D: either 1 Ω or 4 Ω

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Five resistors, each of 4 Ω, are connected to form a square ABCD (one resistor on each side) together with its diagonal AC. The equivalent resistance between the corners B and D is:

solution.concept: Symmetry: points at equal potential carry no current between them
solution.explanation: With the source across B and D, the network is symmetric about the line BD, so A and C are at the same potential and the diagonal AC carries no current. It can be removed.
steps: V_A = V_C by symmetry → no current in AC
Remaining: path B–A–D (8 Ω) in parallel with path B–C–D (8 Ω)
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 Ω is the resistance between A and C (the ends of the diagonal), not between B and D. 8/3 Ω wrongly puts the diagonal in parallel with one 8 Ω path. 8 Ω counts only one path.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors; Wheatstone bridge

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Four identical cells, each of emf ε and internal resistance r, are grouped as described in List-I. Match each grouping with the emf and internal resistance of the combination in List-II.

List-I:
A. All four in series
B. All four in parallel
C. Two pairs, each pair of two cells in series, the two pairs then joined in parallel
D. Three cells in parallel, and this group joined in series with the fourth cell

List-II:
I. 2ε and r
II. 4ε and 4r
III. 2ε and 4r/3
IV. ε and r/4

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Cells in series and in parallel
solution.explanation: In series, emfs and internal resistances add. Identical cells in parallel keep the emf of one cell and divide the internal resistance by their number.
steps: Parallel of four: ε, r/4 → B-IV
Each pair: 2ε, 2r; two pairs in parallel: 2ε, r → C-I
Three in parallel: ε, r/3; in series with one cell: 2ε, r/3 + r = 4r/3 → D-III
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes swap the series and parallel results or give the two-pair grouping the internal resistance of the 3 + 1 grouping.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells in series and in parallel
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Resistors are connected across an ideal battery (no internal resistance) whose emf stays constant, and the resistances do not change with temperature. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) When two resistors R₁ > R₂ are in series across the battery, more heat is produced per second in R₁.
(b) When the same two resistors are in parallel across the battery, more heat is produced per second in R₂.
(c) Connecting one more resistor in parallel across the battery increases the total power drawn from it.
(d) Connecting one more resistor in series with a resistor already across the battery increases the current drawn from it.
(e) Two identical bulbs in series across the battery together consume one-fourth of the power that one bulb consumes when connected alone across it.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Power in series and parallel combinations: P = I²R and P = V²/R
solution.explanation: In series the current is common, so P = I²R is larger for the larger resistance. In parallel the voltage is common, so P = V²/R is larger for the smaller resistance. Adding a parallel branch lowers the total resistance and raises the power V²/R_eq; adding a series resistor raises the total resistance and lowers the current.
steps: (c) True: R_eq falls, P = V²/R_eq rises
(e) False: together they take V²/2R, i.e. half (each bulb alone takes one-fourth)
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) include a false statement; the remaining option leaves out a true one.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors; electrical power

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long air-cored solenoid is 50 cm long and has 500 turns. It carries a current of 2.0 A. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnetic field well inside the solenoid, near its middle, is about:

solution.concept: Field inside a long solenoid: B = µ₀nI, n = turns per unit length
solution.explanation: Ampere's law applied to a rectangular loop half inside the solenoid gives a uniform field µ₀nI inside, where n is the number of turns per metre.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.3 × 10⁻³ T uses the total number of turns N instead of n. 6.3 × 10⁻⁴ T multiplies by the length instead of dividing. 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ T takes n as 1 turn per millimetre but treats it as 1 per metre.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the solenoid

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: An electron moves with a speed of 3.0 × 10⁶ m/s in a direction making an angle of 30° with a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. Taking e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the magnitude of the magnetic force on the electron is:

solution.concept: Magnetic force on a moving charge: F = qvB sin θ
solution.explanation: Only the component of velocity perpendicular to the field contributes to the magnetic force.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N leaves out sin θ. 8.3 × 10⁻¹⁴ N uses cos 30°. Zero would be true only if the velocity were parallel or antiparallel to the field.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A bar magnet of magnetic moment 2.0 A m² is held in a uniform magnetic field of 0.15 T with its axis at 30° to the field. The magnitude of the torque acting on it is:

options.text: zero, because the field is uniform

solution.concept: Torque on a magnetic dipole: τ = m × B, |τ| = mB sin θ
solution.explanation: A uniform field exerts no net force on a magnet but does exert a torque that tends to align m with B.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.30 N m leaves out sin θ. 0.26 N m uses cos 30°. A uniform field gives zero net force, not zero torque.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet: the dipole in a uniform magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A flat circular coil of 100 turns, each of radius 5.0 cm, carries a current of 0.40 A. The magnitude of its magnetic dipole moment is about:

solution.concept: Magnetic moment of a coil: m = NIA
solution.explanation: Each turn is a current loop of moment IA; the N turns add.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.1 × 10⁻³ A m² leaves out the number of turns. 1.26 A m² uses 10 cm (the diameter) as the radius. 12.6 A m² uses the circumference 2πr in place of the area.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the magnetic dipole moment of a current loop

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: The magnetic field lines of a bar magnet form closed loops. Inside the magnet, the field lines run:

options.text: from the north pole to the south pole
from the south pole to the north pole
nowhere, because the magnetic field inside a magnet is zero
radially outwards from the centre of the magnet

solution.concept: Magnetic field lines are continuous closed loops
solution.explanation: Outside the magnet the lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole. Since they form closed loops and do not start or end at the poles, inside the magnet they continue from the south pole to the north pole.
steps: Lines are closed loops → inside: S → N
solution.why_others_wrong: N to S describes the lines outside the magnet. The field inside is not zero. Radial lines would require a magnetic monopole at the centre.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the magnetic field lines
solution.final_answer: Option B: from the south pole to the north pole

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: According to the Biot–Savart law, the magnetic field dB produced at a point P by a small current element I dl is zero when:

options.text: the line joining the element to P is perpendicular to dl
P is very close to the current element
P lies on the line along which the current element points
the current in the element is steady

solution.concept: Biot–Savart law: dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl × r/r³, magnitude ∝ sin θ
solution.explanation: The field of a current element is proportional to sin θ, where θ is the angle between dl and the displacement r to the point. On the line of the element θ = 0° or 180°, so dB = 0.
steps: P on the line of dl → θ = 0 or 180° → dB = 0
solution.why_others_wrong: When r is perpendicular to dl, sin θ = 1 and the field is largest. Close to the element the field is large, not zero. A steady current does produce a field.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field due to a current element, Biot–Savart law
solution.final_answer: Option C: P lies on the line along which the current element points

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A moving-coil galvanometer has a coil of 100 turns, each of area 2.0 cm², in a radial magnetic field of 0.50 T. The torsional constant of its spring is 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ N m rad⁻¹. The steady deflection of the coil for a current of 2.0 mA is:

solution.concept: Moving-coil galvanometer: kφ = NIAB
solution.explanation: In the radial field the deflecting torque NIAB is balanced by the restoring torque kφ of the spring, so the deflection is proportional to the current.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 rad converts cm² to m² with 10⁻² instead of 10⁻⁴. 0.10 rad is the current sensitivity, the deflection per milliampere. 5.0 rad inverts the ratio (k/NIAB).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the moving coil galvanometer

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A short bar magnet produces magnetic fields of equal magnitude at a point P₁ on its axis and at a point P₂ on its equatorial line (the perpendicular bisector of its axis). The ratio of the distances of P₁ and P₂ from the centre of the magnet, r₁ : r₂, is:

solution.concept: Fields of a short magnet: axial B = µ₀(2m)/(4πr³), equatorial B = µ₀m/(4πr³)
solution.explanation: At the same distance the axial field is twice the equatorial field, so the axial point must be farther away for the two to be equal; the fields fall as 1/r³.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 1 forgets the cube. 1 : 2^(1/3) puts the axial point nearer, which would make its field even larger. √2 : 1 treats the field as falling off as 1/r².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long straight wire carries a steady current of 5.0 A. An electron moves parallel to the wire, in the same direction as the current, at a distance of 10 cm from it, with a speed of 4.0 × 10⁶ m/s. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the magnetic force on the electron is:

options.text: 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁸ N, directed away from the wire
1.28 × 10⁻¹⁷ N, directed away from the wire

solution.concept: Field of a straight wire B = µ₀I/(2πd); force on a moving charge F = qv × B
solution.explanation: The field of the wire circles round it, so it is perpendicular to the electron's velocity. A positive charge moving along the current would be pulled towards the wire (like parallel currents); the negative electron is pushed away.
steps: Electron moving along the current ≡ conventional current opposite to the wire's → repelled, away from wire
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Towards the wire' is the direction for a positive charge. 1.28 × 10⁻¹⁷ N uses µ₀I/(πd), twice the field. Zero assumes the field is along the wire, but it circles the wire and is perpendicular to the velocity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field of a straight wire; Lorentz force
solution.final_answer: Option B: 6.4 × 10⁻¹⁸ N, directed away from the wire

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long straight cylindrical wire of radius R carries a steady current spread uniformly over its cross-section. The ratio of the magnetic field at a distance R/2 from its axis to the field at a distance 2R from its axis is:

solution.concept: Ampere's law inside and outside a long current-carrying cylinder
solution.explanation: Inside, a circular Amperian loop of radius r encloses the fraction r²/R² of the current, so B ∝ r. Outside, it encloses all of it, so B ∝ 1/r.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 4 and 4 : 1 use the 1/r law (or the r law) at both points. 1 : 2 uses B ∝ r inside but forgets that the field outside falls off with distance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A charged particle at rest in a uniform magnetic field B experiences a magnetic force of magnitude qB.
Statement II: The magnetic force on a moving charged particle is directed along its velocity.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Magnetic part of the Lorentz force: F = q(v × B)
solution.explanation: The magnetic force depends on the velocity: F = qvB sin θ, which is zero for v = 0. Because it is a cross product, the force is perpendicular to v (and to B), never along v.
steps: F = q(v × B) ⊥ v → Statement II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are false, so every other option is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a bar magnet is cut into two halves by a cut perpendicular to its length, each half is a complete magnet with a north pole and a south pole.
Reason (R): Isolated magnetic north and south poles (magnetic monopoles) exist and can be separated by cutting a magnet.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Magnetic poles always occur in pairs
solution.explanation: Cutting a bar magnet gives two smaller magnets, each with both poles, however many times it is cut. This is because isolated magnetic poles (monopoles) are not known to exist. A is true; R is false.
steps: Each piece is a magnet with N and S → A true
Monopoles do not exist → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false, so options A, B and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The magnetic field well inside a long solenoid is nearly uniform and parallel to its axis.
(b) The magnetic field at points in the open space outside an ideal toroid is zero.
(c) For a fixed number of turns per unit length and a fixed current, the field inside a long solenoid increases as the solenoid is made longer.
(d) Ampere's circuital law, ∮B·dl = µ₀I, holds for steady currents.
(e) Ampere's circuital law is valid only for circular closed paths.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Ampere's circuital law and its applications
solution.explanation: Ampere's law holds for any closed loop around steady currents; circles are chosen only when symmetry makes the integral easy. For a long solenoid B = µ₀nI depends only on n and I, not on the length. Outside an ideal toroid an Amperian loop encloses no net current, so the field there is zero.
steps: (b) True: no net current enclosed outside
(c) False: B = µ₀nI, independent of length
(d) True: the law is for steady currents
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options include (c) or (e), which are false, or leave out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law; the solenoid; the toroid

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long, straight, insulated wire carrying a steady current I is bent, in one plane, so that it forms a single complete circular loop of radius R. The straight parts of the wire lie along one line that touches the loop at the point where the loop begins and ends, and the wire turns smoothly into the loop and out of it without any kink, so that the current continues along the straight line in its original direction. The magnitude of the magnetic field at the centre of the loop is:

solution.concept: Superposition of the fields of a circular loop and a long straight wire
solution.explanation: The straight wire is effectively an infinitely long wire at distance R from the centre. Because the wire runs smoothly into the loop, the current at the point of contact has the same direction in the loop as in the straight part, so both produce fields at the centre in the same direction (perpendicular to the plane).
steps: Straight wire at distance R: B₂ = µ₀I/(2πR)
solution.why_others_wrong: (1 − 1/π) assumes the two fields oppose, which would need the loop current to reverse direction at the contact point. µ₀I/(2R) ignores the straight wire. (1 + 2/π) uses µ₀I/(πR) for the straight wire.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', field on the axis of a circular loop; Ampere's law (straight wire)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. A rectangular loop carrying a current of 2.0 A lies in the same plane, with its two 10 cm long sides parallel to the wire at distances of 5.0 cm and 15 cm from it. In the side nearer the wire, the loop current is in the same direction as the current in the wire. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the net magnetic force on the loop is:

solution.concept: Force between parallel currents: F = µ₀I₁I₂L/(2πd)
solution.explanation: The two sides perpendicular to the wire carry opposite currents at the same distances, so their forces cancel. The near side (current parallel to the wire's) is attracted; the far side (antiparallel) is repelled, but less strongly because it is farther away.
steps: Near side: F₁ = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 10 × 2.0 × 0.10/0.05 = 8.0 × 10⁻⁶ N, towards the wire
Far side: F₂ = 2 × 10⁻⁷ × 10 × 2.0 × 0.10/0.15 = 2.67 × 10⁻⁶ N, away from the wire
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Away from the wire' reverses the net direction. 1.07 × 10⁻⁵ N adds the two forces although they are opposite. 8.0 × 10⁻⁶ N counts only the near side.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', force between two parallel currents
solution.final_answer: Option C: 5.3 × 10⁻⁶ N, towards the wire

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: Two identical short bar magnets, each of magnetic moment 1.0 A m², lie in a horizontal plane with their centres 20 cm apart on a line XY. Magnet 1 lies along XY and magnet 2 is perpendicular to XY. Ignoring all other magnetic fields and taking µ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the resultant magnetic field at the midpoint of the line joining their centres is about:

solution.concept: Axial and equatorial fields of a short magnet; vector addition
solution.explanation: The midpoint is 10 cm from each centre. It lies on the axis of magnet 1 and on the equatorial line of magnet 2. The axial field of magnet 1 is along XY; the equatorial field of magnet 2 is antiparallel to its own moment, i.e. perpendicular to XY. The two fields are at right angles.
steps: Magnet 2 (equatorial): B₂ = 10⁻⁷ × 1.0/(0.10)³ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ T, perpendicular to XY
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ T adds the magnitudes as if the fields were parallel. 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ T subtracts them. 2.8 × 10⁻⁴ T treats the midpoint as an axial point of both magnets.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', the bar magnet as an equivalent solenoid

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Like the electrostatic field of a point charge, the magnetic field of a current element is long-range and falls off as the inverse square of the distance from it.
Statement II: The electrostatic field of a point charge is along the line joining the charge to the field point, whereas the magnetic field of a current element is perpendicular to the plane containing the element and the line joining it to the field point.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Comparison of the Biot–Savart law with Coulomb's law
solution.explanation: dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl × r/r³ has magnitude ∝ 1/r², like Coulomb's law, so both fields are long-range. The electrostatic field is radial, along r, but dB is along dl × r, perpendicular to the plane of dl and r. There is also an angle factor (sin θ) in the magnetic case.
steps: E along r; dB along dl × r → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so every other option is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Biot–Savart law (comparison with Coulomb's law)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A particle of charge q and mass m moves with speed v at right angles to a uniform magnetic field B, in a circle of radius r. Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II.

List-I:
A. Radius of the circle
B. Time period of revolution
C. Frequency of revolution
D. Kinetic energy

List-II:
I. q²B²r²/(2m)
II. 2πm/(qB)
III. mv/(qB)
IV. qB/(2πm)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Circular motion of a charge in a magnetic field
solution.explanation: The magnetic force supplies the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB). The period 2πr/v = 2πm/(qB) is independent of speed, and the frequency is its reciprocal. Using v = qBr/m in ½mv² gives the kinetic energy in terms of r.
steps: v = qBr/m → K = ½mv² = q²B²r²/(2m) → D-I
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping B and C confuses the period with the frequency. The other codes put the radius or the kinetic energy against the wrong expression.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about a plane circular loop of radius R carrying a steady current I are correct?

(a) For a fixed current, the magnetic field at the centre of the loop is inversely proportional to R.
(b) At points on the axis far from the loop (distance x ≫ R), the field falls off as 1/x³.
(c) The loop behaves as a magnetic dipole of moment IA, where A is the area of the loop.
(d) Doubling the radius of the loop, with the current unchanged, doubles its magnetic moment.
(e) The magnetic field at the centre of the loop lies in the plane of the loop.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Field of a circular current loop; the loop as a magnetic dipole
solution.explanation: On the axis, B = µ₀IR²/[2(R² + x²)^(3/2)]. At the centre (x = 0) this is µ₀I/(2R) ∝ 1/R; for x ≫ R it becomes µ₀IR²/(2x³) = µ₀(2m)/(4πx³) with m = IπR², the field of a dipole. The field at the centre is along the axis, perpendicular to the plane of the loop.
steps: (d) False: A = πR² → m becomes 4 times
(e) False: B at centre is perpendicular to the plane
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes (d) or (e), which are false, or leaves out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop; the magnetic dipole

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A flat coil of 50 turns, each of area 0.020 m², is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T. The field makes an angle of 60° with the plane of the coil. The total magnetic flux linked with the coil is about:

solution.concept: Magnetic flux: Φ = BA cos θ, θ measured from the normal to the coil
solution.explanation: The angle in Φ = BA cos θ is between B and the area vector (the normal). A field at 60° to the plane is at 30° to the normal. Flux linkage counts every turn.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.25 Wb uses the 60° angle (with the plane) in cos θ. 0.50 Wb ignores the angle. 8.7 × 10⁻³ Wb is the flux through one turn only.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', magnetic flux

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal inductor of inductance (0.2/π) H is connected to a 220 V (rms), 50 Hz AC supply. The rms current in the circuit is:

solution.concept: Inductive reactance X_L = ωL = 2πfL; I_rms = V_rms/X_L
solution.explanation: A pure inductor limits the current through its reactance, which grows with frequency.
solution.why_others_wrong: 15.6 A uses the peak voltage (220√2) with an rms answer. 7.8 A divides the rms value by √2 again. 22 A uses πfL (half the reactance).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to an inductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The coil of an AC generator has 100 turns, each of area 0.050 m², and rotates at 50 revolutions per second about an axis perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.20 T. The peak emf induced in the coil is about:

solution.concept: AC generator: ε = NBAω sin ωt, peak ε₀ = NBAω
solution.explanation: The flux through the rotating coil varies sinusoidally, and the peak emf is NBAω with ω = 2πν.
solution.why_others_wrong: 50 V uses ω = 50 rad/s (the revolutions per second) instead of 2πν. 3.14 V leaves out the number of turns. 222 V is the rms value, not the peak.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', AC generator

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A closed coil is placed near various sources. In which of the following situations is NO emf induced in the closed coil?

options.text: A bar magnet is moved towards the coil
A neighbouring coil carries a steady current, and both coils are at rest
The steady current in a neighbouring coil is switched off
The coil is rotated in a uniform magnetic field about an axis in its plane, perpendicular to the field

solution.concept: Faraday's law: an emf is induced only when the magnetic flux linked with the coil changes
solution.explanation: A steady current in a stationary neighbouring coil produces a constant flux through the coil, so no emf is induced. Moving a magnet, switching a current off and rotating the coil all change the flux.
steps: Steady current + no motion → constant flux → no emf
Every other case changes the flux → emf induced
solution.why_others_wrong: Each of the other situations changes the flux linked with the coil (by motion of the magnet, by change of current, or by change of orientation), so an emf is induced.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', the experiments of Faraday and Henry
solution.final_answer: Option B: A neighbouring coil carries a steady current, and both coils are at rest

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 30 Ω resistor and a capacitor of reactance 40 Ω are connected in series to a 200 V (rms) AC supply. The rms voltages across the resistor and across the capacitor are, respectively:

solution.concept: Series RC circuit: Z = √(R² + X_C²); voltages add as phasors
solution.explanation: Find the current from the impedance; each element's rms voltage is the current times its own resistance or reactance. The two voltages are 90° out of phase, so they do not add up to 200 V arithmetically.
solution.why_others_wrong: 86 V and 114 V share 200 V in the ratio 3 : 4 as if the voltages added arithmetically. 160 V and 120 V are swapped. 150 V and 200 V take the current as 200/40 = 5 A, ignoring the resistor in the impedance.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit (phasor diagram)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In an AC circuit, the rms voltage is 220 V and the rms current is 5.0 A, the current lagging behind the voltage by 60°. The average power consumed and the wattless component of the current are, respectively:

solution.concept: Average power P = V_rms I_rms cos φ; wattless current I_rms sin φ
solution.explanation: Resolve the current into a component in phase with the voltage (I cos φ), which carries the power, and a component 90° out of phase (I sin φ), which consumes no average power: the wattless current.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.5 A is I cos φ, the power-carrying (wattful) component. 950 W uses sin φ for the power. 1100 W leaves out the power factor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', power in AC circuit: the power factor (wattless current)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a series LCR circuit connected to an AC source, the rms voltages across the resistor, the inductor and the capacitor are 40 V, 80 V and 50 V respectively. The rms voltage of the source is:

solution.concept: Phasor addition: V = √[V_R² + (V_L − V_C)²]
solution.explanation: V_L and V_C are opposite in phase, so they partly cancel; their difference is at 90° to V_R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 170 V adds the three voltages arithmetically. 70 V adds V_R to (V_L − V_C) arithmetically. 102 V adds the squares of all three, treating V_L and V_C as perpendicular.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit (phasor diagram)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Self-inductance plays the role of inertia in an electric circuit; it is the electrical analogue of mass in mechanics.
Reason (R): The self-induced emf in a coil opposes any change (growth or decay) of the current in it.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Self-induction and electrical inertia
solution.explanation: Mass resists a change of velocity; a coil's self-induced back emf, −L dI/dt, resists a change of current. Because self-inductance opposes changes of current just as mass opposes changes of motion, it is called the electrical inertia. R gives the reason for A.
steps: Back emf ε = −L dI/dt opposes change of current → R true
This opposition to change is what makes L analogous to mass → A true and explained by R
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the very property that makes the analogy hold, so B is wrong; both are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', self-inductance
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In a purely resistive AC circuit, the average power dissipated is V_rms × I_rms.
Statement II: An alternating current of peak value I₀ produces the same heating effect in a resistor as a steady current of value I₀.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: rms values and power in AC circuits
solution.explanation: For a resistor the current is in phase with the voltage, so P = V_rms I_rms (power factor 1). The steady current with the same heating effect is the rms value I₀/√2, not the peak value I₀.
steps: Resistor: φ = 0, P = V_rms I_rms → Statement I true
Average power = I₀²R/2 = (I₀/√2)²R → equivalent DC is I₀/√2 → Statement II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is true and Statement II is false; the other combinations are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to a resistor
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Each circuit in List-I is connected to a sinusoidal AC source. Match it with the phase relation between the current and the source voltage in List-II.

List-I:
A. A pure resistor
B. A pure inductor
C. A pure capacitor
D. A resistor and a capacitor in series, with resistance R equal to the capacitive reactance X_C

List-II:
I. Current leads the voltage by π/4
II. Current lags behind the voltage by π/2
III. Current is in phase with the voltage
IV. Current leads the voltage by π/2

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Phase relations in AC circuits
solution.explanation: Current and voltage are in phase in a resistor. In an inductor the current lags by π/2; in a capacitor it leads by π/2. In a series RC circuit tan φ = X_C/R, with the current leading; for X_C = R, φ = π/4.
steps: RC with X_C = R: tan φ = 1, leads by π/4 → D-I
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping B and C reverses the inductor and capacitor. The other codes give the RC circuit a phase of 0 or π/2, which needs X_C = 0 or R = 0.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to an inductor and to a capacitor
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two long vertical conducting rails, 0.40 m apart, are joined at the top by a 2.0 Ω resistor. A uniform horizontal magnetic field of 0.50 T is perpendicular to the plane of the rails. A horizontal conducting rod of mass 20 g slides down the rails without friction, always in contact with them. Neglecting all other resistances and taking g = 10 m/s², the terminal speed of the rod is:

solution.concept: Motional emf ε = Bvl; magnetic force on the induced current opposes the motion (Lenz's law)
solution.explanation: As the rod falls, the induced current I = Bvl/R experiences an upward force BIl = B²l²v/R that grows with speed. The rod stops accelerating when this force equals its weight.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 m/s uses Bl instead of B²l². 2.5 m/s puts R in the denominator. 4 m/s squares B but not l.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', motional electromotive force; energy consideration

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A resistor R, an inductor L and a capacitor C are available. When R and L alone are connected in series to an AC source of fixed frequency, the current lags the voltage by 45°. When R and C alone are connected in series to the same source, the current leads the voltage by 45°. When R, L and C are all connected in series to this source, the power factor of the circuit is:

solution.concept: Phase angle tan φ = (X_L − X_C)/R; power factor cos φ
solution.explanation: A 45° phase difference in the RL circuit means X_L = R; in the RC circuit, X_C = R. In the LCR circuit the two reactances cancel, so the circuit is at resonance.
steps: LCR: Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²] = R → cos φ = R/Z = 1
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/√2 is the power factor of either two-element circuit, not of the full LCR circuit. 1/2 and zero do not follow from equal reactances; zero would need R = 0.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit; resonance; power factor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Each circuit in List-I is connected to an AC source. Match it with its power factor in List-II.

List-I:
A. A pure inductor
B. A pure resistor
C. A resistor R in series with a capacitor of reactance √3 R
D. A series LCR circuit with X_L = 2R and X_C = R

List-II:
I. 1/2
II. zero
III. 1/√2
IV. 1

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Power factor cos φ = R/Z
solution.explanation: Use Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²] for each circuit. A pure reactance has R = 0 and power factor zero; a pure resistance has Z = R.
steps: LCR: X_L − X_C = R → Z = √2 R → 1/√2 → D-III
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping A and B gives the inductor the power factor of a resistor. Swapping C and D, or B and C, mismatches the RC and LCR results.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', power in AC circuit: the power factor
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A series LCR circuit (R ≠ 0) is driven by an AC source of fixed rms voltage whose frequency can be varied. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) At resonance, the voltages across the inductor and the capacitor are equal in magnitude and opposite in phase.
(b) At resonance, the amplitude of the current is the largest.
(c) A series circuit containing only a resistor and an inductor (no capacitor) can also be brought to resonance by changing the frequency.
(d) The resonant frequency of the circuit depends on the resistance R.
(e) At resonance, the average power drawn from the source is V_rms²/R.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Resonance in a series LCR circuit
solution.explanation: At ω₀ = 1/√(LC), X_L = X_C, so the voltages across L and C cancel, Z = R is a minimum and the current is a maximum. Resonance needs both L and C, since the reactances must cancel. ω₀ does not involve R. At resonance the power factor is 1, so P = V_rms I_rms = V_rms²/R.
steps: (c) False: needs both L and C
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options include (c) or (d), which are false, or leave out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit: resonance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The remote switches of household electronic systems such as TV sets work by sending out:

solution.concept: Uses of infrared radiation
solution.explanation: Infrared radiation is produced by light emitting diodes and is used in the remote switches of household electronic systems such as TV sets, video recorders and hi-fi systems.
steps: Remote controls use IR LEDs → infrared
solution.why_others_wrong: Ultraviolet is used, for example, to kill germs; microwaves are used in radar and ovens; gamma rays come from nuclear reactions and are used in medicine. None of these is used in TV remote switches.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum (infrared waves)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An electromagnetic wave of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz travels through a non-magnetic medium (relative permeability 1) of relative permittivity 2.25. Its speed in the medium is v = c/√(µ_r ε_r), with c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s. The wavelength of the wave in the medium is:

solution.concept: Speed of an EM wave in a medium: v = 1/√(µε) = c/√(µ_r ε_r); λ = v/f
solution.explanation: The frequency is fixed by the source; in the medium the speed and hence the wavelength are reduced by the factor √(µ_r ε_r) = 1.5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 600 nm is the wavelength in vacuum. 267 nm divides by ε_r instead of √ε_r. 900 nm multiplies by 1.5 instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves (speed in a medium)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The electric field between the plates of a parallel-plate capacitor, each of area 0.050 m², is uniform and is increasing at the rate of 2.0 × 10¹² V m⁻¹ s⁻¹. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the displacement current between the plates is about:

solution.concept: Displacement current: i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt = ε₀ A dE/dt
solution.explanation: The changing electric flux between the plates acts as a source of magnetic field, just like a conduction current of value ε₀ dΦ_E/dt.
steps: Φ_E = EA → dΦ_E/dt = A dE/dt = 0.050 × 2.0 × 10¹² = 1.0 × 10¹¹ V m s⁻¹
solution.why_others_wrong: 17.7 A leaves out the plate area. 354 A divides by the area instead of multiplying. 1.3 × 10⁵ A uses µ₀ in place of ε₀.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: A displacement current exists in a region only when the electric flux through that region changes with time.
Statement II: While a capacitor is being charged, the displacement current between its plates is equal to the conduction current in the connecting wires.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Maxwell's displacement current
solution.explanation: i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt is zero for a steady electric field. During charging, the conduction current i brings charge Q to the plates, and the flux between them is Q/ε₀, so i_d = ε₀ d(Q/ε₀)/dt = dQ/dt = i: the total current (conduction plus displacement) is continuous.
steps: i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt → zero if Φ_E is constant → Statement I true
Φ_E = Q/ε₀ → i_d = dQ/dt = i → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so every other option is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The critical angle C for light travelling from a transparent medium into air is such that sin C = 3/5. Taking the speed of light in air as 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the speed of light in the medium is:

solution.concept: Critical angle: sin C = 1/n; speed v = c/n
solution.explanation: The critical angle fixes the refractive index of the medium relative to air, and the refractive index fixes the speed of light in it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.0 × 10⁸ m/s multiplies by n instead of dividing (and exceeds c). 2.4 × 10⁸ m/s uses cos C. 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s assumes the speed does not change.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An object is placed 5 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 10 cm. The image formed is:

options.text: 10 cm in front of the mirror, real, with magnification −2
3.3 cm behind the mirror, virtual, with magnification +0.67
10 cm behind the mirror, virtual, with magnification +2

solution.concept: Mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f with the Cartesian sign convention; m = −v/u
solution.explanation: An object inside the focus of a concave mirror gives a virtual, erect, magnified image behind the mirror.
solution.why_others_wrong: '10 cm in front, real' drops the sign of v. 3.3 cm comes from adding 1/10 and 1/5 (magnitudes without signs). 'At infinity' is the case of an object at the focus.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', the mirror equation; magnification
solution.final_answer: Option D: 10 cm behind the mirror, virtual, with magnification +2

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The power of a thin lens is −2.5 D. Its focal length and the type of lens are:

solution.concept: Power of a lens: P = 1/f, with f in metres
solution.explanation: Power in dioptres is the reciprocal of the focal length in metres; a negative power means a diverging lens.
solution.why_others_wrong: −0.4 cm leaves the answer in metres but labels it centimetres. +40 cm ignores the sign of the power. −4 cm divides 10 by 2.5.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', power of a lens
solution.final_answer: Option A: −40 cm; a concave (diverging) lens

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ray of light in air falls on the plane surface of a glass block of refractive index √2 at an angle of incidence of 45°. The angle through which the ray is deviated from its original direction on entering the glass is:

solution.concept: Snell's law: sin i = n sin r; deviation at one surface = i − r
solution.explanation: The ray bends towards the normal; the deviation is the angle between the incident and refracted directions.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30° is the angle of refraction, not the deviation. 45° is the angle of incidence. 75° adds i and r.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ falls normally on a single polaroid, which is slowly rotated in its own plane. The intensity of the light transmitted by the polaroid:

options.text: becomes zero twice in every rotation

solution.concept: Unpolarised light and a polaroid
solution.explanation: In unpolarised light the direction of the electric field changes randomly, so every orientation of the pass axis transmits the same average intensity, half of the incident intensity.
steps: Any orientation transmits I₀/2 → no change on rotation
solution.why_others_wrong: Variation between I₀ and zero is what a second polaroid (analyser) shows when it is rotated in already polarised light; with unpolarised light the transmitted intensity never varies or becomes zero.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation
solution.final_answer: Option B: remains constant at I₀/2

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Light from a distant star reaches the Earth. A small portion of the wavefront arriving at a telescope can be taken to be:

solution.concept: Shapes of wavefronts
solution.explanation: A point source sends out spherical wavefronts. At a very large distance the radius of the sphere is huge, so a small portion of the wavefront is effectively a plane.
steps: Very far from the source, a small part of a large sphere ≈ plane
solution.why_others_wrong: A diverging spherical wavefront is seen close to a point source; a cylindrical one comes from a linear source (such as a slit); a converging spherical wavefront is produced, for example, by a convex lens.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', Huygens principle

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A point object in air lies on the axis of a long glass rod (refractive index 1.5) whose end is ground to a convex hemispherical surface of radius of curvature 10 cm. The object is 30 cm from the pole of this surface. The image formed by refraction at the surface is:

options.text: 18 cm from the pole, inside the glass (real)
60 cm from the pole, inside the glass (real)
90 cm from the pole, inside the glass (real)
45 cm from the pole, on the air side (virtual)

solution.concept: Refraction at a spherical surface: n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R
solution.explanation: Light goes from air (n₁ = 1) into glass (n₂ = 1.5). With the Cartesian convention, u = −30 cm and R = +10 cm (centre of curvature inside the glass).
steps: v = +90 cm: real image inside the glass
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 cm takes u = +30 cm. 60 cm drops n₂ from the term n₂/v. 45 cm (virtual) ignores the curvature, treating the surface as plane.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction at spherical surfaces
solution.final_answer: Option C: 90 cm from the pole, inside the glass (real)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin biconcave lens is made of glass of refractive index 1.6, and both its surfaces have radius of curvature 30 cm. Its focal length in air is:

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula: 1/f = (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
solution.explanation: For a biconcave lens, with light going from left to right, the first surface has its centre of curvature on the incident side (R₁ = −30 cm) and the second on the far side (R₂ = +30 cm).
solution.why_others_wrong: −50 cm counts only one curved surface. +25 cm ignores the signs of the radii, giving a converging lens. −9.4 cm uses n instead of (n − 1).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', lens maker's formula

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 90 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5 cm. It is adjusted so that the final image is formed at the least distance of distinct vision, D = 25 cm. The magnifying power of the telescope is:

solution.concept: Telescope with the final image at the near point: M = (f_o/f_e)(1 + f_e/D)
solution.explanation: With the final image at D instead of at infinity, the eyepiece acts as a simple microscope with magnification (1 + f_e/D) on the angular size set by the objective.
solution.why_others_wrong: 18 is the magnifying power in normal adjustment (image at infinity). 19 adds 1 to f_o/f_e. 14.4 uses (1 − f_e/D).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments: telescope

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment with light of wavelength 600 nm, a certain length of the screen contains exactly 10 fringe widths. If the light is replaced by light of wavelength 400 nm, all else unchanged, the number of fringe widths in the same length of the screen becomes:

solution.concept: Fringe width β = λD/d ∝ λ
solution.explanation: The fixed length equals N × β. Since β is proportional to λ, the number of fringes in that length is inversely proportional to λ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.7 uses N ∝ λ. 10 assumes the fringe width does not depend on wavelength. 22.5 squares the ratio of the wavelengths.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A right-angled isosceles glass prism (angles 90°, 45°, 45°) can be used to turn a beam of light through 90° or through 180° by total internal reflection.
Reason (R): The critical angle for ordinary glass (refractive index about 1.5) is greater than 45°.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Totally reflecting prisms
solution.explanation: In such a prism the light meets the hypotenuse (or the two short faces) at 45° inside the glass. For n = 1.5, sin C = 1/1.5, so C ≈ 41.8°, which is less than 45°; the light is therefore totally reflected. A is true; R is false.
steps: Angle of incidence 45° > C → total reflection → A true
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false (if C were greater than 45°, these prisms would not work), so options A, B and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection (prisms)
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The linear magnification produced by a plane mirror is −1.
Statement II: A convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image of a real object.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Images formed by plane and convex mirrors
solution.explanation: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect image of the same size, so m = +1 (a negative magnification would mean an inverted image). For a convex mirror f > 0 and u < 0, so v is always positive (behind the mirror) and less than f, giving a virtual, erect, diminished image.
steps: Plane mirror: erect, same size → m = +1 → Statement I false
Convex mirror: 0 < v < f for every real object → virtual, erect, diminished → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false and Statement II is true; every other combination is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each quantity in List-I with its expression in List-II (n = refractive index, A = angle of the prism, D_m = angle of minimum deviation, R₁ and R₂ = radii of curvature, f = focal length in metres).

List-I:
A. Refractive index of the material of a prism
B. Deviation produced by a thin prism
C. 1/f for a thin lens in air (lens maker's formula)
D. Power of a lens

List-II:
I. (n − 1)A
II. 1/f
III. sin[(A + D_m)/2]/sin(A/2)
IV. (n − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Prism and lens formulae
solution.explanation: At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically through the prism, giving n = sin[(A + D_m)/2]/sin(A/2). For small A this reduces to D = (n − 1)A. The lens maker's formula gives 1/f, and the power of a lens is 1/f in dioptres.
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping A and B confuses the exact prism formula with its small-angle form. The other codes mismatch the lens maker's formula and the definition of power.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction through a prism; lens maker's formula; power
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about wavefronts are correct?

(a) The wavefront due to a point source at a finite distance is spherical.
(b) Rays are perpendicular to the wavefronts.
(c) According to the wave theory, light that bends towards the normal on refraction travels faster in the second medium.
(d) A thin convex lens converts an incident plane wavefront into a converging spherical wavefront.
(e) A plane wavefront reflected from a plane mirror becomes a spherical wavefront.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Huygens' principle: wavefronts and their propagation
solution.explanation: A point source gives spherical wavefronts and rays are normals to the wavefronts. Huygens' construction gives n₂/n₁ = v₁/v₂, so bending towards the normal (n₂ > n₁) means slower travel in the second medium. A convex lens converts a plane wave into a spherical wave converging to its focus; a plane mirror reflects a plane wave as a plane wave.
steps: (c) False: v₂ < v₁ when the ray bends towards the normal
(e) False: the reflected wavefront is plane
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options include (c) or (e), which are false, or leave out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', Huygens principle; refraction and reflection of plane waves

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A parallel beam of light travelling along the common principal axis falls on a thin convex lens of focal length 10 cm. A thin concave lens of focal length 10 cm is placed coaxially 5 cm behind the convex lens (on the side away from the incoming light). The final image is formed:

options.text: 10 cm beyond the concave lens, real
3.3 cm before the concave lens (on the convex-lens side), virtual
5 cm beyond the concave lens, real

solution.concept: Two-lens system: the image of the first lens is the object for the second
solution.explanation: The convex lens alone would focus the beam 10 cm behind it, i.e. 5 cm beyond the concave lens. The concave lens intercepts the converging beam, so that point is a virtual object for it.
steps: Convex lens: image at +10 cm from it
For the concave lens: u = +5 cm (virtual object), f = −10 cm
1/v = 1/f + 1/u = −1/10 + 1/5 = +1/10 → v = +10 cm: real image 10 cm beyond the concave lens
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.3 cm (virtual) treats the virtual object as a real object (u = −5 cm). 'At infinity' treats the lenses as if they were in contact (net power zero). '5 cm beyond' ignores the concave lens.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', combination of thin lenses
solution.final_answer: Option A: 10 cm beyond the concave lens, real

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small bulb lies at the bottom of a tank filled to a depth of 60 cm with a transparent liquid of refractive index 1.25. Light from the bulb can emerge into the air above only through a circular patch of the liquid surface directly above the bulb. The radius of this patch is:

solution.concept: Total internal reflection: rays meeting the surface at more than the critical angle are trapped
solution.explanation: Light escapes only where the angle of incidence at the surface is less than C. The edge of the patch is where the ray from the bulb meets the surface exactly at C, so r = h tan C.
solution.why_others_wrong: 48 cm uses h sin C. 45 cm uses h/tan C. 36 cm uses h cos C.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the slits are 1.0 mm apart and the screen is 1.0 m away. The slits are illuminated with light containing two wavelengths, 600 nm and 480 nm. The least distance from the central maximum at which a bright fringe of one wavelength falls exactly on a bright fringe of the other is:

solution.concept: Position of the nth bright fringe: y = nλD/d; coincidence when n₁λ₁ = n₂λ₂
solution.explanation: Bright fringes of the two wavelengths coincide where the same path difference is a whole number of each wavelength. The smallest such path difference (other than zero) is the least common multiple of 600 nm and 480 nm.
steps: Smallest: n₁ = 4, n₂ = 5 → path difference 2400 nm
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.6 mm is only the first bright fringe of 600 nm light. 1.08 mm adds the two wavelengths. 4.8 mm is the second coincidence (n₁ = 8, n₂ = 10).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): When a plane wavefront passes through a thin prism, the emerging wavefront is a plane that is tilted with respect to the incident wavefront.
Reason (R): The part of the wavefront that travels through the thicker portion of the prism is delayed more, because light travels more slowly in glass than in air.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Refraction of a plane wave by a prism (Huygens' construction)
solution.explanation: Different parts of the incident wavefront cross different thicknesses of glass. The part crossing the thick base spends longer in the slower medium and lags behind the part crossing near the apex, so the emerging wavefront is tilted (the light is deviated towards the base). R explains A.
steps: Speed in glass < speed in air
