Greater thickness → greater delay → wavefront tilts → A true, explained by R
solution.why_others_wrong: R is the cause of the tilt described in A, so B is wrong; both are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', Huygens principle (refraction of a plane wave by a thin prism)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the diffraction pattern of a single slit of width a, illuminated normally by light of wavelength λ, the angular width of the central maximum is 2λ/a.
Statement II: If the slit is illuminated with blue light instead of red light, all else unchanged, the central maximum becomes wider.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Single-slit diffraction: width of the central maximum
solution.explanation: The first minima lie at θ = ±λ/a (small angles), so the central maximum spans an angle 2λ/a. Since the width is proportional to λ, the shorter wavelength of blue light gives a narrower central maximum.
steps: First minima at ±λ/a → angular width 2λ/a → Statement I true
λ_blue < λ_red → narrower central maximum → Statement II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is true and Statement II is false; the other combinations are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction at a single slit
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about total internal reflection are correct?

(a) It can occur only when light travels from an optically denser medium towards an optically rarer medium.
(b) It occurs only when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle for the pair of media.
(c) For light going from different media into air, the critical angle is larger for a medium of larger refractive index.
(d) When total internal reflection occurs at a boundary, there is no refracted ray in the rarer medium.
(e) For a given glass, the critical angle at a glass–water boundary is smaller than at a glass–air boundary.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Conditions for total internal reflection; sin C = n_rarer/n_denser
solution.explanation: TIR needs denser-to-rarer travel and incidence beyond the critical angle; then all the light is reflected and no refracted ray exists. sin C = n_rarer/n_denser, so a larger n_denser gives a smaller C, and replacing air by water (n closer to that of glass) increases C.
steps: (c) False: sin C = 1/n → larger n, smaller C
(e) False: glass–water: sin C = 1.33/1.5 ≈ 0.89 (C ≈ 63°) > glass–air: sin C = 0.67 (C ≈ 42°)
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options include (c) or (e), which are false, or leave out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Most metals emit photoelectrons only when ultraviolet light falls on them. Which of the following metals emit photoelectrons even when visible light falls on them?

options.text: Alkali metals such as sodium, potassium and caesium
All metals, provided the visible light is intense enough
No metal; visible light can never eject photoelectrons

solution.concept: Threshold frequency depends on the metal
solution.explanation: Alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium, caesium, rubidium) have small work functions and respond even to visible light. Metals such as zinc, cadmium and magnesium respond only to ultraviolet light of short wavelength.
steps: Low work function → threshold in the visible → alkali metals
solution.why_others_wrong: Zinc, cadmium and magnesium need ultraviolet light. Intensity cannot make up for a frequency below the threshold. Alkali metals do emit with visible light, so 'no metal' is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', photoelectric effect (Hallwachs' and Lenard's observations)
solution.final_answer: Option A: Alkali metals such as sodium, potassium and caesium

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Taking Planck's constant h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the momentum of a photon of wavelength 500 nm is:

solution.concept: Photon momentum: p = h/λ
solution.explanation: Every photon of wavelength λ carries momentum h/λ (and energy hc/λ).
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.3 × 10⁻⁴⁰ multiplies h by λ. 1.32 × 10⁻³⁶ leaves λ in nanometres. 3.96 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the photon's energy in joules (hc/λ), not its momentum.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', particle nature of light: the photon

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: The work function of a metal is 2.0 eV. Taking Planck's constant as 4.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s, the threshold frequency for photoelectric emission from this metal is:

solution.concept: Threshold frequency: hν₀ = φ₀
solution.explanation: At the threshold frequency, the photon energy just equals the work function, and the photoelectrons come out with zero kinetic energy.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ Hz divides h by φ₀. 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁵ Hz multiplies them. 5.0 × 10¹⁵ Hz is a slip of a power of ten.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: The stopping potential for photoelectrons emitted from a metal surface is 1.8 V. Taking the electron's charge as 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and its mass as 9 × 10⁻³¹ kg, the maximum speed of the photoelectrons is:

solution.concept: Stopping potential: eV₀ = K_max = ½mv_max²
solution.explanation: The stopping potential is just enough to stop the fastest photoelectrons, so eV₀ equals their maximum kinetic energy.
solution.why_others_wrong: 5.7 × 10⁵ m/s leaves out the factor 2 in √(2K/m). 6.4 × 10¹¹ is v², not v. 4.0 × 10⁵ m/s puts the 2 in the denominator, v = √(K/2m).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', experimental study of photoelectric effect (stopping potential)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Photons of energy 5.0 eV fall on two metal surfaces, P of work function 2.0 eV and Q of work function 4.0 eV. The ratio of the maximum speed of the photoelectrons from P to that from Q is:

solution.concept: Einstein's equation K_max = hν − φ₀; v ∝ √K
solution.explanation: Find each maximum kinetic energy, then remember that speed goes as the square root of kinetic energy for the same particle.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 : 1 is the ratio of kinetic energies, not speeds. 1 : √3 inverts the ratio. 2 : 1 uses the inverse ratio of the work functions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Photoelectrons are emitted from a metal surface only if the energy of each incident photon is at least equal to the work function of the metal.
Reason (R): The work functions of metals are of the order of a few electron volts.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Photon picture of the photoelectric effect; work function
solution.explanation: An electron absorbs one photon and must receive at least the work function to escape, so emission needs hν ≥ φ₀ (A is true). Work functions are indeed a few eV (for example about 2 eV for caesium and about 5 eV for platinum), so R is true. But the size of the work function does not explain why one photon must supply at least φ₀; that follows from the single-photon absorption process. R is not the explanation of A.
steps: One photon is absorbed by one electron; escape needs energy ≥ φ₀ → A true
R states a magnitude; it does not explain the condition in A → option B
solution.why_others_wrong: Option A would need R to give the reason for A, which it does not. Both statements are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', electron emission; photoelectric effect
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Match each case in List-I with its de Broglie wavelength (or wavelength) in List-II. (h = Planck's constant, c = speed of light.)

List-I:
A. A particle of momentum p
B. A particle of mass m and kinetic energy K
C. A particle of mass m and charge q, accelerated from rest through a potential difference V
D. A photon of energy E

List-II:
I. hc/E
II. h/√(2mqV)
III. h/p
IV. h/√(2mK)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: de Broglie relation λ = h/p
solution.explanation: For a particle, p = √(2mK); accelerating a charge q through V gives K = qV. For a photon, E = hc/λ.
solution.why_others_wrong: The other codes exchange the kinetic-energy and accelerating-voltage forms or give the photon a particle formula.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: An electron and a photon each have a wavelength of 0.1227 nm. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm and, for an electron of kinetic energy K (in eV), λ = 1.227/√K nm, the ratio of the energy of the photon to the kinetic energy of the electron is about:

solution.concept: Photon energy E = hc/λ; electron kinetic energy from λ = h/√(2mK)
solution.explanation: The same wavelength means the same momentum, but energy depends on momentum differently: E = pc for a photon and K = p²/2m for the electron.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 assumes the same wavelength means the same energy (it means the same momentum). 10 is roughly the square root of the correct ratio. 1.0 × 10⁴ is the photon energy in eV, not the ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter; the photon

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: A monochromatic beam of light of wavelength 600 nm and power 3.0 W falls normally on a surface that absorbs it completely. Treating the beam as a stream of photons, each of energy hc/λ and momentum h/λ, and taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the force exerted by the beam on the surface is:

solution.concept: Force = rate of transfer of momentum by the photons
solution.explanation: If N photons arrive per second, N(hc/λ) = P and the momentum delivered per second is N(h/λ) = P/c. The wavelength cancels.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ N would apply to a perfectly reflecting surface, where each photon's momentum is reversed. 9.0 × 10⁸ N multiplies P by c. 1.0 × 10⁸ N divides c by P.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', particle nature of light: the photon

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Which of the following are predictions of the wave picture of light that DISAGREE with the observed features of the photoelectric effect?

(a) The maximum kinetic energy of the emitted electrons should increase with the intensity of the light.
(b) Emission should occur at any frequency, provided the light is intense enough.
(c) For very dim light, there should be a noticeable time lag before emission begins.
(d) There should be a threshold frequency below which no emission occurs, however intense the light.
(e) The photocurrent should increase with the intensity of the light.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Failure of the wave picture to explain the photoelectric effect
solution.explanation: In the wave picture, energy arrives continuously and is spread over the wavefront, so a brighter beam should give faster electrons, any frequency should work if intense enough, and dim light should need time to accumulate energy. All three disagree with experiment. A threshold frequency is not a prediction of the wave picture (it is an observation the wave picture cannot explain), and a photocurrent rising with intensity is observed, so it is not a disagreement.
solution.why_others_wrong: Every other option includes (d) or (e), or leaves out one of the three conflicting predictions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', photoelectric effect and wave theory of light

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the energy equivalent of 1 g of matter is:

solution.concept: Mass–energy equivalence: E = mc²
solution.explanation: Einstein's relation gives the energy equivalent of any mass; the mass must be in kilograms.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9 × 10¹⁶ J takes the mass as 1 kg. 3 × 10⁵ J uses mc instead of mc². 9 × 10¹⁰ J converts grams to kilograms with 10⁻⁶.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', mass–energy and nuclear binding energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the Bohr model, the total energy of the electron in the ground state of the hydrogen atom is −13.6 eV. Its kinetic energy and potential energy in this state are, respectively:

solution.concept: Bohr orbit energies: K = −E, U = 2E
solution.explanation: For an electron held in a circular orbit by the Coulomb force, K = ke²/2r and U = −ke²/r, so U = −2K and E = K + U = −K.
solution.why_others_wrong: −13.6 eV for K gives a negative kinetic energy, which is impossible. +27.2 and −40.8 eV, and +6.8 and −20.4 eV, add up to −13.6 eV but do not satisfy U = −2K.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom (energy of the electron)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the alpha-particle scattering experiment, a very small fraction of the alpha particles were deflected through more than 90°, some almost straight back. This observation led Rutherford to conclude that:

options.text: electrons are spread uniformly through a sphere of positive charge
most of the space inside an atom is empty
alpha particles are strongly attracted by the electrons of the atom
the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in a tiny central region

solution.concept: Rutherford's nuclear model
solution.explanation: Turning a fast, heavy alpha particle back needs a very large repulsive force, which is possible only if the positive charge (and most of the mass) is packed into a very small nucleus that the particle can approach closely.
steps: → positive charge and mass concentrated in a tiny nucleus
solution.why_others_wrong: A uniform sphere of positive charge (Thomson's model) cannot produce large deflections. 'Mostly empty space' is concluded from the undeflected particles, not the large-angle ones. Electrons are far too light to deflect alpha particles appreciably.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', alpha-particle scattering and Rutherford's nuclear model of atom
solution.final_answer: Option D: the positive charge and most of the mass of the atom are concentrated in a tiny central region

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, the electron jumps from the n = 4 orbit to the n = 2 orbit. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the magnitude of the change in its orbital angular momentum is about:

solution.concept: Bohr's quantisation condition: L = nh/2π
solution.explanation: The angular momentum in the nth orbit is n times h/2π, so the change between two orbits is (n₁ − n₂)h/2π.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.05 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is a single unit h/2π. 4.2 × 10⁻³⁴ J s is the angular momentum in the n = 4 orbit, not the change. 6.3 × 10⁻³⁴ J s adds the quantum numbers (4 + 2) instead of subtracting.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom (quantisation of angular momentum)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Taking the radius of a nucleus of mass number A as R = R₀A^(1/3) with R₀ = 1.2 fm, and the mass of a nucleon as 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg, the density of nuclear matter is about:

solution.concept: Nuclear density: mass A × m_N divided by volume (4/3)πR₀³A
solution.explanation: Both the mass and the volume of a nucleus are proportional to A, so A cancels and the density is the same for all nuclei.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.6 × 10¹⁷ takes the volume as R₀³, leaving out 4π/3. 2.9 × 10¹⁶ uses 2R₀ (a diameter) as the radius. 2.3 × 10¹⁴ takes 1 fm as 10⁻¹⁴ m.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', size of the nucleus

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): The Bohr model cannot be extended even to two-electron atoms such as helium.
Reason (R): In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, the radius of the nth orbit is proportional to n².

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Limitations of the Bohr model
solution.explanation: The Bohr model applies to hydrogenic (one-electron) atoms; in a two-electron atom each electron interacts with the other electron as well as with the nucleus, which the model cannot handle (A true). The orbit radius r_n ∝ n² is a correct result of the model (R true), but it says nothing about why the model fails for many-electron atoms.
steps: Bohr model fails for He (electron–electron interaction) → A true
R is a property of hydrogen orbits, unrelated to the failure → option B
solution.why_others_wrong: R does not give the reason for A, so option A is wrong; both are true, so C and D are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom (limitations)
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The mass of a stable nucleus is less than the total mass of its protons and neutrons taken separately.
Statement II: The mass of a free neutron is exactly equal to the mass of a proton.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Mass defect and nucleon masses
solution.explanation: Energy (the binding energy) must be supplied to separate a nucleus into free nucleons, so the nucleus is lighter than its separated nucleons by ΔM = E_b/c². The neutron is slightly heavier than the proton (1.00866 u against 1.00727 u).
steps: Mass defect ΔM > 0 for a bound nucleus → Statement I true
m_n ≈ 1.00866 u > m_p ≈ 1.00727 u → Statement II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is true and Statement II is false; the other combinations are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', atomic masses and composition of nucleus; mass–energy and nuclear binding energy
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
For a hydrogen-like ion of atomic number Z in a given orbit n of the Bohr model, match each quantity in List-I with the way it depends on Z in List-II.

List-I:
A. Radius of the orbit
B. Speed of the electron
C. Magnitude of the total energy
D. Time period of revolution of the electron

List-II:
I. Z
II. Z²
III. 1/Z²
IV. 1/Z

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Bohr model for hydrogen-like ions: r ∝ n²/Z, v ∝ Z/n, E ∝ Z²/n²
solution.explanation: A nucleus of charge Ze pulls the electron in more strongly: the orbit shrinks as 1/Z and the speed grows as Z. The energy goes as Z², and the period 2πr/v goes as (1/Z)/Z = 1/Z².
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping C and D gives the energy and the period each other's dependence. The other codes swap the radius and the speed.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Hydrogen atoms in the ground state are excited by monochromatic radiation whose photons each have energy 12.75 eV. Using E_n = −13.6/n² eV, the number of different wavelengths that can be present in the emission spectrum as the atoms return to the ground state is:

solution.concept: Excitation by photon absorption; number of spectral lines from level n: n(n − 1)/2
solution.explanation: A photon is absorbed only if its energy matches a level difference exactly. Find the level reached, then count every possible downward transition, including those through intermediate levels.
steps: E₄ − E₁ = 13.6(1 − 1/16) = 12.75 eV → atoms reach n = 4
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 counts only the direct jumps from n = 4. 4 is the quantum number reached, not the number of lines. 10 would apply to atoms raised to n = 5.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', the line spectra of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A nuclear reactor produces thermal power at the rate of 200 MW. Each fission of a ²³⁵U nucleus releases 200 MeV of energy. Taking 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J, the number of fissions taking place per second is:

solution.concept: Rate of fission = power/(energy per fission)
solution.explanation: Convert the energy per fission to joules, then divide the power (joules per second) by it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 × 10⁶ divides 200 MW by 200 MeV without converting units. 6.25 × 10²⁴ converts MeV as if it were eV. 6.25 × 10¹⁵ takes 200 MW as 200 kW.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', nuclear energy: fission

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) According to classical electromagnetic theory, an electron revolving round the nucleus in Rutherford's model should radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus.
(b) Rutherford's model, combined with classical theory, would predict a continuous emission spectrum rather than a line spectrum.
(c) In the Bohr model, the frequency of the photon emitted in a transition equals the frequency of revolution of the electron in its initial orbit.
(d) An alpha particle aimed head-on at a nucleus (zero impact parameter) rebounds back along its path.
(e) The larger the impact parameter of an alpha particle, the larger the angle through which it is scattered.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Rutherford's nuclear model, its classical difficulty, and the Bohr frequency condition
solution.explanation: An accelerating (revolving) charge radiates classically; the orbit would shrink and the frequency of the emitted radiation would change continuously, giving a continuous spectrum. In the Bohr model the photon's frequency is fixed by the energy difference, hν = E_i − E_f, not by the orbital frequency. In scattering, a head-on alpha particle rebounds (θ ≈ 180°), while a larger impact parameter means a smaller deflection.
steps: (e) False: larger b → smaller scattering angle
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options include (c) or (e), which are false, or leave out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', alpha-particle trajectory (impact parameter); Bohr model of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The barrier potential of a silicon p-n junction is 0.7 V. The effective height of the potential barrier when the junction is forward biased by 0.4 V, and when it is reverse biased by 0.4 V, is respectively:

solution.concept: Effect of bias on the barrier: forward V₀ − V, reverse V₀ + V
solution.explanation: In forward bias the applied voltage opposes the built-in potential and lowers the barrier; in reverse bias it adds to it and raises the barrier.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.1 V and 0.3 V swaps the two cases. 0.7 V and 0.7 V assumes bias does not change the barrier. 0.3 V and 0.3 V subtracts in both cases.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics', p-n junction diode under forward and reverse bias

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A Zener diode has a breakdown voltage of 9.0 V and a maximum power rating of 0.45 W. The largest current it can safely carry in the breakdown region is:

solution.concept: Power in the Zener: P = V_Z I_Z
solution.explanation: In breakdown the voltage across the Zener stays at V_Z, so the current is limited by the power it can dissipate.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 mA comes from V/P = 20, read as milliamperes. 4.05 A multiplies P by V. 5 mA is a slip of a power of ten.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics', Zener diode

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Which one of the following is a compound semiconductor?

solution.concept: Elemental and compound semiconductors
solution.explanation: Silicon and germanium are elemental semiconductors. Compound semiconductors are formed from two or more elements, for example GaAs, CdS, CdSe and InP. Copper is a metal (conductor).
steps: GaAs: compound of gallium and arsenic
solution.why_others_wrong: Silicon and germanium are elemental semiconductors, and copper is a metal.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics', classification of metals, conductors and semiconductors

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The NAND gate is called a universal gate because the basic gates OR, AND and NOT can all be built using NAND gates alone.
Statement II: The output of a two-input NOR gate is 1 only when both its inputs are 0.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: NAND as a universal gate; NOR truth table
solution.explanation: A NAND gate with its inputs joined is a NOT gate; NAND followed by such a NOT gives AND; NOT on each input followed by NAND gives OR. NOR = NOT(A + B), which is 1 only for A = B = 0.
steps: NAND realises NOT, AND and OR → Statement I true
NOR outputs 1, 0, 0, 0 for 00, 01, 10, 11 → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so every other option is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: On the forward characteristic of a junction diode, the current is 10 mA at a forward voltage of 0.70 V and 20 mA at 0.72 V. The dynamic resistance of the diode in this region is:

solution.concept: Dynamic resistance: r_d = ΔV/ΔI
solution.explanation: The diode's I–V characteristic is not linear, so its resistance is defined for small changes about the operating point as the ratio of the change in voltage to the change in current.
solution.why_others_wrong: 70 Ω and 36 Ω are the static ratios V/I at the two points. 0.5 Ω inverts the ratio (ΔI/ΔV).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics', p-n junction diode: V–I characteristics (dynamic resistance)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The primary of a step-down transformer with turns ratio N_p : N_s = 10 : 1 is connected to the 220 V (rms), 50 Hz mains. The secondary feeds a half-wave rectifier consisting of an ideal diode in series with a load resistor. The peak voltage across the load is about:

solution.concept: Transformer ratio, then peak = √2 × rms; an ideal diode passes the positive peak unchanged
solution.explanation: The transformer reduces the rms voltage in the turns ratio. The half-wave rectifier passes alternate half cycles, so the load sees the full positive peak of the secondary voltage.
solution.why_others_wrong: 22 V is the rms value, not the peak. 311 V ignores the transformer. 15.6 V divides by √2 instead of multiplying.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics', application of junction diode as a rectifier

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At a given temperature, an n-type semiconductor contains more holes than the intrinsic semiconductor of the same material.
Reason (R): In thermal equilibrium, the electron and hole concentrations in a semiconductor satisfy n_e n_h = n_i².

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Mass-action law in doped semiconductors
solution.explanation: Doping with donors raises n_e far above n_i. Because n_e n_h = n_i² (R true), n_h = n_i²/n_e falls below n_i: the many electrons recombine with holes. So an n-type sample has fewer holes than the intrinsic one, and A is false.
steps: n_e ≫ n_i → n_h = n_i²/n_e ≪ n_i → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options A, B and C (which need A to be true) are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics', extrinsic semiconductor
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each quantity in List-I with its approximate value in List-II.

List-I:
A. Energy band gap of carbon (diamond)
B. Energy band gap of silicon
C. Energy band gap of germanium
D. Threshold (cut-in) voltage of a germanium junction diode

List-II:
I. about 0.2 V
II. about 5.4 eV
III. about 0.7 eV
IV. about 1.1 eV

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Band gaps of C, Si and Ge; cut-in voltage of a Ge diode
solution.explanation: Diamond has a large gap (about 5.4 eV) and is an insulator; silicon (about 1.1 eV) and germanium (about 0.7 eV) are semiconductors. The forward current of a germanium diode rises sharply beyond about 0.2 V (about 0.7 V for silicon).
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping B and C reverses the band gaps of silicon and germanium. The other codes give diamond a semiconductor's gap or mix up the band gap of germanium with its diode's cut-in voltage.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics', classification on the basis of energy bands; diode V–I characteristics
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about electrons and holes in a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor are correct?

(a) A hole is a vacancy left in a covalent bond, and it behaves as a positive charge carrier.
(b) Electron–hole pairs are produced by thermal energy breaking covalent bonds.
(c) The motion of a hole under an applied field actually results from bound electrons jumping from one covalent bond into a neighbouring vacancy.
(d) Holes are free positively charged particles, of the same mass as protons, released from the nuclei.
(e) In thermal equilibrium, electrons and holes never recombine.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Intrinsic semiconductors: holes, generation and recombination
solution.explanation: Thermal energy frees some electrons from covalent bonds, leaving vacancies (holes) with an effective positive charge. A hole moves when a bound electron from a neighbouring bond fills it, leaving a new vacancy. In equilibrium, the rate of generation equals the rate of recombination of electrons and holes.
steps: (d) False: a hole is not a particle from the nucleus
(e) False: recombination goes on and balances generation
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options include (d) or (e), which are false, or leave out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics', intrinsic semiconductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A Zener diode of breakdown voltage 6.0 V is used as a voltage regulator: a 500 Ω series resistor connects it to a variable DC input, and a 1.2 kΩ load is connected across the Zener. Treating the Zener as drawing current only when the voltage across it would otherwise exceed 6.0 V, the minimum input voltage for which the load voltage stays at 6.0 V is:

solution.concept: Zener regulator: at the edge of regulation the Zener current is zero and the load takes all the current
solution.explanation: At the minimum input, the Zener just reaches breakdown: the series resistor and the load form a voltage divider that puts exactly 6.0 V across the load.
steps: Load current at 6.0 V: I_L = 6.0/1200 = 5.0 mA
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.0 V ignores the drop across the series resistor. 20.4 V inverts the divider ratio (6.0 × (1 + R_L/R_s)). 2.5 V is only the drop across the series resistor.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics', Zener diode as voltage regulator

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Inputs A and B are fed to an AND gate. The output of the AND gate and the input A are then fed to a NOR gate, whose output is Y. The output Y is equal to:

solution.concept: Truth table of a combination of gates
solution.explanation: Y = NOT(A·B + A). Whenever A = 1 the NOR has an input 1, so Y = 0; when A = 0 both NOR inputs are 0, so Y = 1. Hence Y = Ā, whatever B is.
solution.why_others_wrong: B̄ would give 1, 0, 1, 0. NAND gives 1, 1, 1, 0 (it differs at A = 1, B = 0). A + B gives 0, 1, 1, 1.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: Zener breakdown occurs when the Zener diode is forward biased beyond about 0.7 V.
Statement II: In the breakdown region, a large change in the current through a Zener diode produces a large change in the voltage across it.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Zener breakdown and regulation
solution.explanation: Breakdown happens under reverse bias: at the Zener voltage the strong field in the very thin depletion region pulls electrons out of their bonds and the reverse current rises sharply. In this region the voltage stays almost constant over a large range of current, which is why the Zener diode is used as a regulator.
steps: Breakdown is a reverse-bias effect → Statement I false
Large ΔI gives very small ΔV in breakdown → Statement II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are false, so every other option is wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics', Zener diode
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both Statement I and Statement II are false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the V–I characteristics of a p-n junction diode are correct?

(a) Beyond the threshold voltage, the forward current increases very rapidly with a small increase of voltage.
(b) Under reverse bias below breakdown, the current is very small (of the order of µA) and nearly independent of the reverse voltage.
(c) In forward bias, the dynamic resistance of the diode is larger at larger currents.
(d) At forward voltages below the threshold voltage, the forward current is very large.
(e) For a silicon diode, the threshold voltage is about 0.7 V.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Forward and reverse characteristics of a junction diode
solution.explanation: Below the threshold the forward current is negligible; above it the current rises steeply, so ΔV/ΔI (the dynamic resistance) becomes smaller at larger currents. The reverse current is a small minority-carrier current that hardly changes with voltage until breakdown. The threshold is about 0.7 V for silicon (about 0.2 V for germanium).
steps: (c) False: steeper curve → smaller r_d at large current
(d) False: the current is negligible below threshold
solution.why_others_wrong: The other options include (c) or (d), which are false, or leave out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics', p-n junction diode: V–I characteristics

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The main scale of a vernier calipers is graduated in divisions of 0.5 mm, and 20 divisions of the vernier scale coincide with 19 divisions of the main scale. The least count of the instrument is:

solution.concept: Least count = 1 MSD − 1 VSD
solution.explanation: The least count is the difference between one main-scale division and one vernier-scale division.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.05 mm takes a main-scale division as 1 mm. 0.026 mm divides 0.5 mm by 19 instead of 20. 0.5 mm is one main-scale division.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform metre scale balances horizontally on a knife edge placed at its 50.0 cm mark. When an unknown mass is hung at the 10.0 cm mark and a 60 g mass at the 80.0 cm mark, the scale again balances on the knife edge at the 50.0 cm mark. The unknown mass is:

solution.concept: Principle of moments about the knife edge
solution.explanation: The scale's own weight acts at the 50 cm mark, on the knife edge, so it has no moment. The moments of the two hanging masses about the knife edge must be equal.
solution.why_others_wrong: 80 g interchanges the arms. 60 g assumes equal arms. 7.5 g uses the scale readings 10 and 80 as the arms.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'System of Particles and Rotational Motion', principle of moments

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the half-deflection method for finding the resistance G of a galvanometer, the galvanometer, a resistance R = 2100 Ω and a cell of negligible internal resistance are in series, and the galvanometer shows a deflection θ. When a shunt S = 100 Ω is connected across the galvanometer, with R unchanged, the deflection falls to θ/2. The resistance of the galvanometer is:

solution.concept: Half-deflection method: G = RS/(R − S)
solution.explanation: Write the galvanometer current with and without the shunt, and set the second equal to half of the first.
steps: With shunt: I_g′ = [E/(R + GS/(G + S))] × S/(G + S) = ES/[R(G + S) + GS]
solution.why_others_wrong: 100 Ω takes G = S, which holds only when R ≫ G. 95.5 Ω uses RS/(R + S). 2000 Ω is R − S.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In the experiment to verify Ohm's law, the ammeter is connected in series with the resistor and the voltmeter in parallel with it.
Statement II: On the reverse-bias characteristic of a Zener diode, the breakdown voltage is read as the reverse voltage at which the reverse current increases sharply.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Connection of meters; Zener characteristic
solution.explanation: An ammeter must carry the current through the resistor, so it goes in series; a voltmeter must have the same potential difference across it as the resistor, so it goes in parallel. On a Zener's reverse characteristic the current stays tiny until the breakdown voltage, where it rises steeply at almost constant voltage.
steps: Ammeter in series, voltmeter in parallel → Statement I true
Breakdown voltage = knee of the reverse characteristic → Statement II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, so every other option is wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A student tests each component in List-I by connecting it, in series with a low-voltage DC source and a current-indicating meter, first one way round and then the other. Match each component with the observation in List-II.

List-I:
A. Resistor
B. Junction diode
C. Light emitting diode
D. Capacitor (initially uncharged)

List-II:
I. A brief current that dies away to zero; no steady current either way round
II. A steady current in one direction only, and the component glows
III. The same steady current both ways round
IV. A steady current in one direction only, and the component does not glow

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Identifying a resistor, a diode, an LED and a capacitor
solution.explanation: A resistor conducts equally in both directions. A diode conducts in one direction only; an LED also conducts one way only but emits light. A capacitor allows only a momentary charging current and then blocks steady DC.
steps: Resistor: same current both ways → A-III
Diode: one way, no light → B-IV
solution.why_others_wrong: Swapping B and C confuses the diode with the LED. The other codes give the capacitor or the resistor a steady one-way current.
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a resonance-tube experiment with a tuning fork of frequency 500 Hz, the first and second resonances occur at air-column lengths of 16.0 cm and 50.0 cm. The speed of sound in air and the end correction of the tube are, respectively:

solution.concept: Closed pipe with end correction e: l₁ + e = λ/4, l₂ + e = 3λ/4
solution.explanation: Subtracting the two resonance conditions removes the end correction and gives λ/2; putting λ back into the first condition gives e.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 cm forgets to halve (l₂ − 3l₁). 170 m/s takes λ = l₂ − l₁. 320 m/s uses v = 4fl₁, ignoring the end correction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 11 Physics, 'Waves', standing waves in a pipe closed at one end

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the u–v method for finding the focal length of a concave mirror, the image needle is adjusted until there is maximum parallax between it and the image of the object needle.
Reason (R): When there is no parallax between two objects, they are at the same distance from the eye.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Removal of parallax to locate an image
solution.explanation: Two objects at different distances appear to move relative to each other when the eye is moved sideways (parallax). When they are at the same place there is no relative movement (R true). The image needle is therefore adjusted until there is NO parallax with the image, which places it exactly at the image; A is false.
steps: No parallax ⇔ same position → R true
Image needle set for no parallax, not maximum → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false, so options A, B and C (which need A to be true) are wrong.
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.
